title: The World’s Largest Marine Turtle Makes a Move South - Nautilus
content:
Leatherbacks aren’t only spectacular for bodies that rival grand pianos in size and weight, but also for their temperature tolerances. By taking refuge in cool upwellings, they can inhabit tropical waters up to 86°F; on the flip side, by warming their bodies with activity and insulating fat, they can tolerate waters as cold as 32°F. But even leatherbacks have their limits. 

A recent study in the journal Chelonian Conservation and Biology found that warming oceans are shifting the nesting sites of leatherback sea turtles (Dermochelys coriacea) to cooler waters. Typically, the critically endangered population of eastern Pacific leatherbacks concentrates its nesting along the west coasts of Mexico and Costa Rica. Now, though, they’re showing up about 1,000 miles south in Ecuador. 

Read more: “How Sea Turtles Find Their Way”

“Historically, observing female Eastern Pacific leatherbacks on Ecuador’s beaches was a rare or unusual event, but our findings suggest they are adapting their reproductive cycle to thrive and survive in coastal Ecuador,” explained lead study author Juan José Alava, a biologist at Simon Fraser University in Canada.

Alava and coauthors in Ecuador compiled records of leatherback nesting activity along Ecuador’s coast from as far back as 1980. Their compilation included peer-reviewed studies as well as conservation reports, government survey records, and validated social media sightings. They also tracked the El Niño and El Niña events that sway sea surface temperatures.

They found record-breaking numbers of nesting females, with the uptick starting around the year 2000. Hatchling leatherback turtles hadn’t been reported along Ecuador’s coast since 1983. So, the emergence of nests in the winters of 2020 and 2021 in Manabí Province was a cause for celebration. And both 2025 and 2026 saw additional hatching success of nests that were relocated to protected areas.  

“It signals new hope for a subspecies of leatherback on track for extinction in the eastern Pacific within 60 years,” added Alava.

Unfortunately, though, a higher frequency of leatherback strandings has also been observed of late. From 2011 to 2026, at least 35 dead leatherbacks were confirmed to have beached on the Ecuadorian coast. Many of those strandings were associated with injuries from fisheries and other human activities.

And so, Pacific leatherbacks haven’t quite found safe harbor yet.

title: Joe Biden’s New Memoir Shows a Man in Denial
author: @NewYorker
content:
The last time Joe Biden published a memoir, called “Promise Me, Dad,” nine years ago, he ended up getting his ghostwriter, Mark Zwonitzer, in a certain amount of trouble. Zwonitzer had recorded interviews he conducted with Biden, including one in February, 2017, at Biden’s rental home in Virginia, in which the then former Vice-President told him, “I just found all the classified stuff downstairs!” That recording would eventually become public because more classified stuff would later be found at a University of Pennsylvania office that Biden used, and then still more at his Delaware home, leading to the appointment of a special counsel, Robert Hur, in 2023. Zwonitzer was subpoenaed, had his computer taken, faced the prospect of criminal charges, and was referred by House Republicans for contempt of Congress. Years of litigation ensued.

Zwonitzer, who also worked with Biden on a 2007 memoir, “Promises to Keep,” is not mentioned in the former President’s latest offering, “Promise Me, America,” which is out next week. (Judging from the acknowledgments, Biden relied on a number of people this time, among them Ted Widmer, a historian whose recent work includes a volume on the Declaration of Independence and an oral history of the band Wings.) Biden gives an account of the classified-documents investigation that focusses, instead, on his rage at Hur, who wrote, in his final report on the case, that the President came across, in his interview with the special counsel, as a “sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory.” Biden calls this “extraneous commentary” and a “gratuitous hit.” It was neither. Biden’s forgetfulness was a reason that Hur cited for not prosecuting the President: if a jury believed that Biden had honestly forgotten about the classified documents, it would have been hard to get a conviction.

By any reckoning, the question of Biden’s general competency during his Presidency is a crucial one; doubts about his fitness ended his campaign for reëlection, after all. But “Promise Me, America” treats all such inquiries as extraneous and gratuitous, not just Hur’s. Biden allows that his June, 2024, debate with Donald Trump (who had his own issues with classified documents) had “gone badly” but adds that “debates had gone badly for lots of incumbent Presidents.” He sees no qualitative distinction between his frightening and heartbreaking lack of focus that night and Barack Obama’s subpar performance against Mitt Romney, or George W. Bush being “caught with a scowling face” in his debate with John Kerry: “The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate.” Biden continues to find it unfair that he was not afforded that opportunity. He blames “the narrative” and disloyal Democrats for the fact that he had to drop out, which he did three and a half weeks after the debate. “I wasn’t living in a dream world,” he writes. “I believed I was the best person to lead the world.”

Incredibly, Biden sticks to that position, even though, in May, 2025, when his second term would have barely been under way, he announced that he had been diagnosed with Stage IV prostate cancer. The disease had metastasized to his bones and, based on what is known as its Gleason score of nine, was fast-moving. His doctors, it emerged, had stuck to the general practice of not routinely screening men older than seventy. (Biden turned eighty in 2022.) In his memoir, Biden answers the question of whether this was wise when the patient was the Commander-in-Chief with a resounding “maybe.” He adds that he was surprised that people were “cynical” enough to think that he might not have been honest about his health. (In February, 2024, three weeks after the Hur report, that same medical team declared him “healthy, active, robust” and “fit for duty.”) It took an interview with People magazine this week to wrest from him the concession that, had he known he had advanced cancer, he wouldn’t have run. “But that wasn’t the case,” he said, still insisting that on “an objective basis” he was the right man for the job. The People interview has been his only one tied to the release of the memoir; in an X post, he said that there wouldn’t be a traditional press tour because the cancer treatment sometimes “slows me down.”

The news of the memoir, in short, is that there is no real news: Biden is as stubbornly in denial as ever. And that assessment risks making the book sound more interesting than it is. Apart from the few, frustrating stretches on his reëlection decision (from which one would never know that he had once referred to himself as “a bridge,” a phrase widely understood to mean that he would serve only a single term), most of “Promise Me, America” is startlingly dull. Much of it has the feel of something written by a committee—and a committee of which Biden himself need not have been a member. Even the headline-making detail, from an early excerpt, in The Atlantic, that on entering the White House in January, 2021, Biden found a note from Trump that was more friendly and circumspect than one would expect from a man who had been trying to overturn the election—“I know how much you love the American people”—is of marginal interest, and really about Trump, not Biden. The advance Biden received for the book was reportedly about ten million dollars.

There are whole pages that read as if someone simply sat down with Biden’s public schedule and speeches and patched them together with a few judicious additions of the first person (“As I said in my welcoming remarks . . .”) and references to America’s past (Lincoln, the gold rush, D Day). A description of a meeting in the Situation Room includes the names and job titles of a dozen people, followed by nothing much illuminating about how they may have interacted or clashed, or about how power in the White House actually worked. Some attendance lists are compelling in themselves, such as the log of phone calls that Biden made in the hours after he dropped out. (Bill Clinton is on it; Obama is not.) But when intimate details about encounters with senators or world leaders do appear, they too often have footnotes that lead to contemporary press coverage or public statements. The source listed for Angela Merkel’s blunt criticism of Trump, for example, is a Guardian article about her memoir. Instead of any real introspection, we get cliché. After a mention of threats posed by China and Russia: “Given these choppy waters, I was glad to be steering the ship of state.”

One of the themes of Biden’s memoir is that he was a fantastic President. To hear him tell it, as his term was coming to an end, things were going great all around. The global economy was “humming,” inflation in the U.S. was falling, we’d “completely rebuilt NATO” and “reclaimed the American advantage over China,” carbon emissions were poised to plunge, and the A.I. companies had meekly fallen in line with his call for them to be more responsible actors. And there were real successes. It would be a far better book if he acknowledged some failure other than not retaining the loyalty of Democratic leaders.

For example, as part of his claim to have beaten COVID, he writes that it took him just four months, until May, 2021, to go “from fewer than half of America’s schools being open to 99 percent.” If that number is news to many parents, it is because Biden seems to be defining “open” as a school where a child showed up at some point, rather than consistently or full time, and ignoring reclosures in the wake of the Omicron variant. (An earlier book, Franklin Foer’s “The Last Politician,” explored the role Joe Biden’s relationship with teachers’ unions played in the struggle to reopen schools, for better or worse.)

There is similar sleight of hand in his discussion of immigration. Biden boasts of a dramatic fall in “encounters with undocumented migrants” at the border between January, 2021, and January, 2025. At the same time, the Biden years did see a historic wave of immigration, and the memoir offers little insight into how it was managed. For example, he does not mention his Administration’s concurrent extension or renewal of Temporary Protected Status to more than a million people, and of humanitarian parole to hundreds of thousands more, many of whom were fleeing terrible circumstances. Those migrants were documented, but, because T.P.S. grants and parole are executive-branch actions, Biden also left them vulnerable to having their status stripped away by the next Administration—which it promptly began doing, as Trump turned migrants into targets.

“Yes, people could point to moments when I mixed up names or lost my train of thought or had a weak voice or walked slowly,” Biden writes. “But they could never point to something presidential that I failed to do.” A few pages later, he points to one. It is the spring of 2024, several months after Hamas brutally murdered civilians in Israel, including at a music festival, taking many of the survivors hostage, and Biden has repeatedly spoken to Benjamin Netanyahu to express his “concerns” about the Israeli military response, and what “rising casualties were doing to Israel’s image.” To his dismay, he writes, “Bibi had no qualms about making promises he had no power—or intention—to keep.” Be that as it may, it also appears that the promises Netanyahu made—to act with restraint, to protect civilians—were ones that Biden no longer had the strength or resolve to enforce. The combination of an ever-mendacious Netanyahu and an increasingly diminished Biden was a disastrous one. In many situations, a good team of staff members can act on behalf of a President, but there are moments when a President is required to impose his or her will, as only a President can. That moment came for Biden after October 7th, and he missed it.

Biden’s wife, Jill Biden, published her own memoir earlier this year. To read them side by side is to be reminded that there is more than one way of being avoidant. Jill padded her book with details about the White House’s floral arrangements; Joe does so with a six-page list of laws he signed, including the CHIPS and Science Act and the Working Dog Health and Welfare Act. The Biden Administration did accomplish a great deal—the legislation passed, the trillions of dollars spent—but it could be notably lacking in transparency, and the President’s memoir doesn’t much help. He speaks more kindly of his Vice-President, Kamala Harris, than Jill does, for example, but without giving a real sense of her influence or why he thought that she would be ready to step in for him, either when he chose her as his running mate or when he endorsed her, twenty-seven minutes after he withdrew from the race.

Where the Jill and Joe memoirs converge is in their repeated, deeply felt invocations of Biden’s older son, Beau, who died of brain cancer in 2015. (Both Bidens also view the younger, troubled Biden son, Hunter, as a martyr-like target of partisan attacks; neither expresses regret for Joe’s decision to grant him, along with other relatives and allies, a broad pardon before leaving office.) Beau’s appearances are the most Bidenesque part of “Promise Me, America,” and the places where Biden’s own mark is most clear. The promise in “Promise Me, Dad,” the 2017 memoir, was Beau’s request that Joe not be so undone by his death that he withdrew from politics.

Beau is also part of Biden’s explanation for his enduring anger at Robert Hur, who said in his report that Biden didn’t know what year it was that Beau died. In his memoir, Biden calls this claim “outrageous,” adding, “if Robert Hur wants to know when my son died, here’s my answer: Today. I wake up every day feeling like I just lost him a minute ago.” But the transcript of their interview shows that Hur was correct. The Hur report matters because, in retrospect, it offered Democrats an opening to replace Biden on the ticket, at a time when only four states had held primaries, and Super Tuesday was still a month away, making it less likely that a decent President would be replaced by an awful one. But it matters in assessing Biden’s memoir, too.

Throughout his career, Biden’s signature rhetorical subject has been how a person pushes on in the face of grief and mourning. As a young man, he lost his first wife and his baby daughter in a car crash. He had it in him to write a great book about the loss of his own powers as he aged, and how it led him to lash out at people like Hur, who said what they saw, and at allies who loved him but knew that he was done. He might have found a way to be grateful for a debate that, aberration or not, insured that he wouldn’t take the oath of office with an undiagnosed case of cancer, and regretful that he didn’t depart the stage even sooner. That this memoir is not that book is a literary as well as a political tragedy. The one thing Biden doesn’t know how to mourn, it seems, is his Presidency. ♦

title: Watch Norway’s Lice-Zapping Robots Protect Salmon Farms - Nautilus
content:
Humans and bears aren’t the only animals that find salmon delicious. Salmon lice, small marine crustaceans, attach themselves to the fish and make a meal of their blood, mucus, and skin cells (not my favorite part of the salmon, but it takes all types). These parasites are also the scourge of Norwegian salmon farmers, who keep their shoals in net pens in the Atlantic Ocean. 

Removing them is required by law, but it’s a real pain. They’ve become resistant to pharmaceutical deterrents and traditional delousing methods involve hot water baths, scrubbing, and general rough handling, which can damage or kill the fish. While some farms have employed cleaner wrasses to feed on the bloodsuckers, they’ve proved difficult to keep alive. 

Read more: “Cocaine Fish: How Salmon Behave When Amped Up on Coke”

So what can be done? 

Obviously the only solution is zapping the parasites with a high-powered laser guided by artificial intelligence. At least that’s what the company Stingray Marine Solutions AS came up with. According to the company, their optical delousing system is already watching over 20 to 25 percent of farmed Norwegian salmon. 

The system consists of robotic “submarines” that float in the net pens. The robots bathe the salmon in blue light to enhance the contrast of the lice against the salmon skin which allows the artificial intelligence to detect the parasites. Once the target is acquired, a high-powered laser capable of firing five pulses per second superheats the louse, killing it. 

It looks incredibly cool in action:  

But does it work? 

Per a study the company paid for, it does. A team of their own researchers combined public data on weekly lice counts and treatments from 845 Norwegian sites with the manufacturer’s records of which sites and weeks used optical delousing. They found sites with the laser system in place required fewer additional delousing treatments compared to sites without them. “Our results show that sites relying on optical delousing exhibit a 50 percent lower weekly treatment probability,” the researchers wrote. 

However, a survey of salmon farmers conducted by the Norwegian Veterinary Institute found mixed results. According to their results, 75 percent of salmon farmers had experience with lasers, and 17 percent of those said they helped them avoid at least one or two delousing treatments. But 56 percent of laser-using farmers said they weren’t sure if they were having any effect. In open-ended questions, the farmers reported the systems were better at delousing when lice populations were low. Additionally, some said the software may be undercounting the parasites (compared to manual counting), which makes their effectiveness difficult to determine.

So lasers may not be the ultimate solution to Norway’s salmon lice problem (yet). But they do look cool doing their jobs.

title: Southern Democrats Repudiate MAGA Racism
author: @NewYorker
content:
Since the 2024 Presidential race, Donald Trump has wrapped himself in the argument that white people are the real victims of racism. This January, in the lead-up to Martin Luther King, Jr., Day, Trump went even further, claiming that the protections initiated in the sixties under the Civil Rights Act led to white people being treated “very badly.” Trump’s acolytes have parroted his claims of white victimhood as an explanation for downward mobility and hardship. Vice-President J. D. Vance has repeatedly claimed that white men, in particular, are victims of racial discrimination. In the closing crescendo of the midterm campaign, much of his venom was directed at Michigan’s Democratic candidate for senator, Abdul El-Sayed, who, Vance said, had “hatred in his heart” for the state’s people and places. “Perhaps,” Vance added, “it’s because he sees them as too white or too proud or too American.”

Apparently, there is an expiration date on the red-meat racism of Trumpism. El-Sayed defeated his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, by seven points. Elsewhere, Republicans attempted to link Black candidates to chaos and crime, but these tried-and-true tactics appear to have had little effect. Angie Nixon, a Florida state representative and union organizer, ran an upstart campaign for the U.S. Senate, and was subject to witheringly racist attacks from the President and his supporters. Laura Loomer, who boasts of her access to Trump, described Nixon as “a ghetto, black, communist.” She mocked Nixon’s speech as “Ebonics” and wrote, “Maybe I need to bark at you and tug your leash and then you’ll finally understand.” Trump said of Nixon, “She’s not of the intellect that should be running for the Senate. She’s a very-low-I.Q. person.” Yet Nixon—who ran a campaign centered on Medicare for All, universal child care, and taxing billionaires—came within three points of defeating the Republican incumbent, Ashley Moody, converting an estimated six per cent of Floridians who voted for Trump in 2024.

In the Georgia gubernatorial race, the Democratic candidate, Keisha Lance Bottoms, was pitted against the Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire health-care executive who spent more than two hundred million dollars of his own money on the election. Bottoms, who served as the mayor of Atlanta during Trump’s first term, gained prominence during those years as one of the President’s opponents: she denied ICE the right to hold detainees in the city’s jail, in response to the Administration’s family-detention practices, and opposed the rapid reopening of Georgia at the height of the pandemic. Jackson, a white man, repeatedly blamed Bottoms for violent crime in Atlanta and for the 2020 unrest in response to police brutality—often conflating the two. Not to be outdone, Trump held a rally outside of Macon, where he accused Bottoms of having “destroyed Atlanta with her crime and filth and constant riots.” She won the race by nearly nine percentage points, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of any state. Across Georgia, seven other Black women won statewide seats.

In Louisiana, Jamie Davis, a third-generation Black farmer, ran for the Senate on what he called the “four pillars” of affordability, education, health care, and upholding the Constitution. He also supported a moratorium on building new data centers and pledged to introduce legislation barring elected officials from signing nondisclosure agreements. According to a local news investigation, his opponent, Representative Julia Letlow, signed an N.D.A. with Meta about a fifty-billion-dollar data-center project in her district; she went on to purchase stock in Meta and then failed to disclose those trades for more than a year, in violation of federal law. (In response to the reporting, a spokesperson for Letlow said that these purchases were made by a broker and that she did not direct any of her trades.)

Astonishingly, Davis was neck and neck with Letlow well into the fall, when, in an act of desperation, a Republican PAC released an ad showing an A.I.-generated Davis lumbering toward the camera in a T-shirt and jeans. A Louisiana Republican pollster, Bernie Pinsonat, explained to a local Fox News affiliate that the ad was intended “to turn any whites off that would think about voting for him. You know, we do have a lot of RINOs”—Republicans in Name Only—“in this state.” Davis came within two points of Letlow, losing by a mere twenty-five thousand votes. The Fox News Voter Poll for Louisiana estimates that he earned the support of ninety-two per cent of Black voters, thirty-four per cent of white voters, and eleven per cent of people who said they had voted for Trump in 2024. Every parish shifted toward Democrats by at least nine points.

The outcome may well have been different had Davis received meaningful assistance from the national Democratic Party. Days before the election, the longtime Democratic Party consultant and Louisiana native son James Carville noted, “I beat my head against the wall trying to get some national money in here. It’s almost impossible.” Scott Colom, the Democratic Senate candidate in Mississippi, whose exceedingly close race was called in his favor on Wednesday, was also left out in the cold. In July, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee made a forty-million-dollar investment in ten Senate battlegrounds, part of which funded outreach to Black voters, that did not include Mississippi—even though a poll had shown that Colom was within three points of the Republican incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith. Finally, the D.S.C.C. joined Colom on a five-hundred-thousand-dollar ad buy with just six days left to vote.

Even near-misses, such as Jamie Davis’s and Angie Nixon’s Senate bids, convey a larger truth about the midterm elections. Two years after Trump’s return, his appeals to white supremacy and victimhood can’t compensate for voters’ struggles with the cost-of-living crisis, disgust with Trump’s corruption, or rage at the billionaires’ prerogative to put data centers anywhere they please. In races across the South, Democratic candidates attracted the support of a wide swath of voters. Their campaigns are evidence of the viability of class politics in every corner of the country. In Mississippi, a remarkable nine per cent of residents who voted for Trump in 2024 voted for Colom in 2026. In Louisiana, one field organizer for Davis said, “I’ve never worked with Republicans this much. Ever.”

The G.O.P.’s racist attacks may not have worked to turn out white voters, but they undoubtedly helped to mobilize Black voters. These date back to the Administration’s war on D.E.I.—specifically, its attack on Black workers in the federal government, led by Elon Musk and the short-lived DOGE. By September, 2026, federal employment had fallen by roughly three hundred and twenty-eight thousand jobs since Trump took office. Multiple lawsuits have alleged that the firings targeted Black workers, who made up roughly eighteen per cent of the federal workforce in 2024. (The Trump Administration has responded that its firings were not racially biased.) The attacks on Black employment were amplified by the continued evisceration of the Voting Rights Act. After the Supreme Court’s Callais decision, in April—which allowed states to redraw, or “crack,” districts that concentrated Black voters to assure their representation—Louisiana dismantled its second majority-Black congressional district, Tennessee split Memphis’s Black communities among three districts, and Alabama reinstated a map that reduced Black voters’ share of the voting-age population in its Second Congressional District.

Just two years ago, Republicans boasted about their new currency with Black men and Latino voters. But the A.P. Voter Poll estimates that, this year, about ninety per cent of Black voters supported Democratic House candidates; roughly eighty per cent backed Kamala Harris in 2024. Only about ten per cent of Black male voters supported Republican candidates, just two years after approximately twenty-five per cent cast ballots for Trump. In Louisiana, where the Callais case originated, Black voters cast more than eighty-six thousand early and absentee ballots—an eighty-three-per-cent increase from the 2022 midterms.

In Alabama, Representative Shomari Figures, a Democrat, won reëlection in the cracked Second Congressional District by nearly eight points. The candidates in Louisiana’s cracked Sixth District are headed to a runoff election. In Tennessee, the Democratic state representative Justin J. Pearson ran in a newly configured district, which previously was centered on Memphis and now stretches over roughly two hundred miles, only to lose by some twenty-five hundred votes to his Republican opponent. In fourteen of the fifteen counties making up the new seat, Republican majorities voted for Trump in the 2024 election. Across these counties, Pearson won 48.5 per cent of the vote.

Pearson is a longtime progressive activist, but not all of these candidates are on the left—Davis ran as a gun-toting farmer and business owner. Nearly all of them, however, campaigned on the affordability crisis, which extends far beyond the cost of gas. Their campaigns upend the assumption of many Democratic consultants that rural and Southern outposts are a poor use of financial resources and political talent. Whether they mark a political turning point will depend upon whether Democrats now choose to take the whole of America, and especially the South, seriously. If Party leaders invest in the Southern candidates who are attracting Black, white, and brown voters and rebuilding regional political organizations, they may find the source of a sustained electoral turnaround. If they do not, we can expect right-wing forces to reassemble a possibly more dangerous version of Trumpism—more serious, more determined, and more destructive. ♦

title: Black Friday Mattress Deals Are Already Wide Awake
author: @wired
content:
Mattress sales come and go so often that it’s hard to determine what’s an actual deal. The times of year when we see the most legit mattress deals are Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Memorial Day, and Labor Day. And this year is no different. We’re already seeing our favorite WIRED-tested bedding and mattress brands offering Black Friday deals leading up to the big weekend. I’ll be on the lookout for more deals as we approach the actual event, so be sure to check back often for fresh discounts on these often-pricey purchases. Note that all mattress prices below are for queen sizes, and discounts on Shop may only appear once you're in the checkout menu.

Want more deals? Check out our guide to the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Amazon, the Best Early Black Friday TV Deals, and Black Friday Deals at Home Depot. Plus, read our related shopping guides to ensure you’re making the most of Black Friday sales, including how to avoid scams and sketchy wares on Amazon, Amazon Prime perks you might not know about, and Black Friday shopping tips.

title: This $48 e-paper display can be whatever you want it to be
content:
Skip to content

Seeed Feed

This DIY e-paper display works in two official ecosystems or on your own server.

Credit: Nick Indge

Credit: Nick Indge

One of the most useful gadgets in my kitchen is now a screen that never asks me for anything.

I recently bought a $48 DIY display kit from Seeed Studio (yes, that’s three E’s), developed in collaboration with TRMNL, that lets me display whatever I want, using whichever software ecosystem I prefer.

I previously built something similar by modding a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, which was selling for around $30 on eBay during a liquidation. The Lenovo device was only ever intended for business-to-business video, but it does a decent job of running a fork of LineageOS. Unfortunately, its limited RAM makes it sluggish. So when I came across the TRMNL kit and its e-paper display, I was sold.

I’d have an always-on display that shows me the information I want, with no subscription required. And since the screen populates automatically, I would never have to wrestle with a slow interface.

The Seeed Studio kit and TRMNL ecosystem aren’t trying to compete with products like the recently announced Apple HomeView, a $299 home hub designed to get the whole family interacting with it. If anything, the TRMNL kit is the HomeView’s antithesis. It’s designed to be entirely passive: The e-paper display stays on, cycling through potentially useful information on your desk or in your kitchen, from calendars and weather to news and all sorts of ideas thought up by its community members.

Here’s how it works.

Choosing a path

TRMNL, the platform company, was founded by indie hardware enthusiast Ryan Kulp in 2023. Its first e-paper device launched via crowdfunding in 2024.

Seeed Studio provides the hardware. The established Shenzhen open hardware company is best known for its XIAO microcontroller boards.

In March 2025, Seeed teased an XIAO e-paper panel on social media, prompting a community member to ask whether it could run TRMNL firmware. The question brought the two teams together, and in July 2025, they announced an official partnership to develop a DIY e-paper kit combining Seeed’s hardware designs with TRMNL’s firmware packages.

Seeed designs and manufactures the hardware, while TRMNL maintains the firmware, plugins, and hosted service. But you’ll still need to make some decisions about how to set up the kit. There are three ways to get it running, depending on your budget and how comfortable you are with managing software yourself.

The stock TRMNL setup connects you with the company’s “BYOD ecosystem” (bring your own device), letting you use trmnl.com as your information server with a 14-day free trial. After that, you’ll need to pay a one-time $50 license fee to keep your device connected to TRMNL servers.

If you’d rather go your own way, Seeed offers software options, including Home Assistant compatibility, that don’t require a TRMNL connection or license. You can also access the SenseCraft Seeedash platform, which includes a plugin repository and design workspace. It’s worth checking out the options before committing to a $50 TRMNL license. The browser-based platform also includes a firmware-flashing tool Seeed describes as simple enough for anyone to use.

If you already have a server up and running, you can point the device right at it. Terminus is TRMNL’s open source container for this setup. The Terminus GitHub page describes the BYOS as providing “privacy first functionality by empowering you to run your own private server, network, and devices. You own the stack and the data.”

The e-paper display and control board simply ping an API to retrieve the information to display. You can even write plugins in HTML, which the screen renders as a bitmap. The trade-off is that your server needs to stay online, and maintaining it may bring some system-admin headaches some users may want to avoid. But hey, that’s why there are options.

An example of a weather app on the Seeed firmware.

What’s in the box?

  • XIAO ePaper Display Dev Board with XIAO ESP32-S3 Plus onboard
  • 7.5-inch monochrome ePaper display (800 × 480 pixels)
  • FPC extension cable (10 cm)
  • FPC connector
  • 2,000 mAh rechargeable Li-ion battery
  • Wi-Fi antenna

Two official case designs are available for 3D printing: a triangular prism and an L-shaped case. I went for the latter, and although I’d hoped assembly would be as simple as plugging everything in and slotting the pieces into place, it proved to be a bit more involved.

The kit came with all the hardware I needed, with one slight hiccup: I’d forgotten to order a case or display stand. Fortunately, TRMNL is a proper DIY project, and there are print files available for recommended stand setups. A quick print at my local library’s Bambu printer and $8 solved the problem. I probably should have chosen something other than “dealer’s choice” for the PLA color, as I ended up with a bright canary yellow device case. At least it stands out on my kitchen countertop.

I’d recommend trying the prism shell design over the L-style case I chose because the latter required me to cut a channel for the ribbon cable extension. It wasn’t a huge deal for a project like this, but you may need to do some extra work and fiddle with the fit. You’ll also need needle-nose pliers to remove the print’s support trees from the narrow space.

Assembly

Before trying to fit everything into the printed case, I wanted to make sure the hardware worked, so I connected the parts on my workbench. The case-less assembly couldn’t be simpler: Connect the battery or a USB-C power source, plug the display directly into the board, and you’re good to go. From there, connect your phone or tablet to the device’s Wi-Fi and enter your local Wi-Fi credentials.

If you attempt this build, be aware that it involves some delicate parts. The FPC is extremely fragile and can break if you force it to bend in a direction it doesn’t want to go (say, around the sharp angle of an L-shaped case). Getting the cable to conform to the design was challenging; I tried using tweezers to coax the cable around the bend but got nowhere fast.

Connecting and routing the ribbon cable extension was the most stressful part of the assembly. The case design just doesn’t accommodate the path the ribbon cable naturally wants to take. Following a helpful tip from a commenter on MakerWorld, I managed to snake the cable through the narrow passage by attaching a bit of paper tape to the end of the ribbon connector.

After powering on the kit for the first time, you’ll see the TRMNL logo and a QR code on the e-paper display. Scanning the code redirects you to a “How to set up a new device” guide written by Kulp, the TRMNL creator. The guide had been updated just 15 minutes before I clicked the link—a promising sign of a living document that is constantly evolving.

TRMNL.com

I wasn’t planning to use the trmnl.com service, but I wanted to get a sense of what it offered for its $50 access fee. The 14-day “free” trial is a misnomer, though. Before you can register your device, you’ll need to enter your credit card information and pay $1 for access. After plopping down a buck, the next screen welcomed me to my trial.

After registering your kit’s MAC address with trmnl.com, you’ll receive what the service calls a “friendly code,” a much shorter identifier that’s easier to remember than an entire MAC address. From there, you can install plugins to display content on a schedule throughout the day.

The options are vast. The marketplace contains standard fare like Google Calendar, weather, and stock quotes, alongside more niche offerings like rotating factoids about the Ferengi Rules of Acquisition in Star Trek.

If you’re looking for a hassle-free solution that “just works,” it’s hard to fault the package trmnl.com has put together. I’m a fan of any service that offers a one-time license fee over yet another forever subscription, and I think $50 is a fair price for the people behind the platform to be compensated for their work. After all, it handles all the rendering; the device simply displays information pulled from the APIs.

SenseCraft

On the Seeed side, there’s SenseCraft, a similar marketplace to trmnl.com’s but without the license fee. The website offers a browser-based flashing tool that promises to “flash official firmware from the browser. No coding. No terminal. Just clicks.”

The process was as simple as promised—once I figured out that I needed a USB-C to USB-C cable. I connected the board to my PC via the onboard USB-C port, opened the website in a Chromium-based browser (sorry, Firefox), selected my device from a drop-down menu, and clicked “Flash.” Once the device rebooted, setup followed essentially the same process as it did with TRMNL, minus the credit card. The tradeoff for free access is that Seeed is based in China and operates under its own privacy policy. Your call, but it’s certainly nice to have options.

After registering a Seeed account, I entered a code displayed on the device, just as I had with TRMNL. SenseCraft’s marketplace is similarly packed with community contributions, but I had trouble determining which plugins were intended for my device and which might not be compatible. I tried publishing several different feeds to the display, but I couldn’t get them to render.

SenseCraft leans heavily into AI-powered custom designs. While the platform offers a bit of everything, much of its content is geared toward the Chinese market, with English-language apps sprinkled throughout. I can see why US users reached out to ask about TRMNL compatibility.

Bring your own server

As TRMNL puts it, “the goal isn’t for BYOS to match parity with our hosted solution but to provide enough of a pleasant solution for your own customized experience.” Even a modest homelab server should have no trouble running the Terminus package, which acts as an API point that takes in information, renders the designs, and sends them to your e-paper display. The process shouldn’t put meaningful strain on most systems.

It’s great that there’s an “easy” version for a fee, but homelabbing is one of my favorite hobbies, and I love self-hosting projects wherever possible. When I first saw the DIY TRMNL/Seeed package, I was hoping I’d be able to control the feed myself.

For now, getting Terminus running on your server isn’t as simple as heading to your OS’s Docker app store and downloading a host service. TRMNL has a great guide to walk you through the setup, but if you’re not comfortable working with docker compose files, you may want to pay the one-time license fee and leave the hosting to TRMNL.

I won’t lie: I spent some late nights banging my head against the desk trying to get everything running. I’d initially tried hosting it on my main Unraid machine, but I kept running into bridge networking issues. The Terminus package is a multi-container compose stack with pieces like Sidekiq worker, Postgres, Valkey, and a certificate initializer. If those containers can’t communicate with each other, nothing works.

Thankfully, I’m a weird nerd who also runs a CasaOS deployment on another machine. After I executed the bin/setup script there, everything worked as it should. The next issue was flashing back to the latest TRMNL firmware package. My unit arrived with FW 1.5.12, well behind the current 1.8.18 release.

Flashing proved to be an annoyance again because I struggled to keep the unit in flashing mode and get the web flasher to communicate with the serial port on my Fedora PC. After about 30 minutes of troubleshooting without making progress, I switched to my MacBook Pro, where the process worked on the first try. Go figure.

Once you’ve updated the display to the proper firmware and pointed its connections at your server, you can write and design your own display templates. If starting from scratch isn’t your thing, TRMNL’s own plugins repo and a community-maintained catalog are available. A new Extensions Gallery in the Terminus web UI lets you import certain plugins for local hosting.

The options are almost overwhelming, and I imagine it will take some time to get everything dialed in exactly as I want it. I still plan to stick with the BYOS route, but the process isn’t as straightforward as I had hoped. For example, the setting for pointing the display at your local server is hidden under the “advanced” settings page during the web portal login.

Real-world impressions

Once I deployed the display in my kitchen, I could get a better sense of how it would fit into my day-to-day life. The 7.5-inch e-paper display is large enough to read from across the room, and all the plugins I had running looked crisp and legible. My son was enamored with the lunar cycles display and commented that “now I’ll always know what moon we have.”

That’s where the kit shines: showing little rotating bursts of useful information that you might never have thought to look up before.

Seeed Studio says the display can run for three months on battery power. I haven’t had the device long enough to verify that claim, but I’m not sure I need the battery for much more than backup. The device powers via USB just fine, so I’ll probably leave it connected to a nearby hub on the counter. The three-month estimate assumes that the display will update once every six hours. I prefer refreshes closer to once an hour, which would cut battery life significantly. Either way, the battery becomes largely irrelevant if you use a USB power source.

Final thoughts

The official TRMNL route is starting to look mighty tempting if it means getting the type of headache-free, set-it-and-forget-it Ron Popeil experience I was expecting from this setup. I’ll keep tinkering with the BYOS solutions, but since those still run on the official TRMNL firmware, I may switch back and use the rest of my 14-day trial to see what best suits my needs. The $50 license fee would push my total project cost over $100. That’s not a huge deal, but it’s double what I was expecting.

The TRMNL/Seeed Studio collaboration has produced a true DIY device. It will never compete with a home assistant device from Amazon or Apple, but it’s not meant to, and that’s a good thing. Not everyone wants a digital butler waiting for their next command. Sometimes you just want information that’s relevant to you and your life, displayed in a central place in your home.

Nick Indge is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica covering hardware, embedded systems, and self-hosted infrastructure. A former security investigator turned tech writer, he writes to help readers escape subscription traps and regain ownership of their digital lives. He lives in Chicagoland with his family and a goofball husky.

title: President Trump's Defamation Claim Against BBC Can Go Forward
content:
From today's decision by Judge Jeffrey Kuntz (S.D. Fla.) in Trump v. BBC:

In Trump v. CNN (S.D. Fla. 2023), aff'd (11th Cir. 2025), Judge Singhal concluded that "the complained of statements are opinion, not factually false statements, and therefore are not actionable." In Trump v. Dow Jones & Co., Inc. (S.D. Fla. 2026), Judge Gayles dismissed President Trump's claims that the Wall Street Journal failed to adequately investigate claims it reported.

Those cases involved a news entity reporting on a story. Here, the news entity created the story. BBC admitted as much by confirming it had edited a video to make it appear as though President Trump made a statement he never made.

And it acknowledged it chose to release the video in a documentary only a week before the 2024 Presidential Election, at the time it would have the most impact. To make sure it was seen in Florida, BBC even emailed U.S. and Florida based commenters with instructions to on how to view the documentary.

Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day. For now, after careful review, and being otherwise fully advised, BBC's Motion to Dismiss is denied [as to the defamation claim] ….

On October 28, 2024, one week before the 2024 Presidential Election, BBC broadcast a documentary titled "Trump: A Second Chance." In the Documentary, a twelve-second segment portrayed President Trump giving a speech to his supporters on January 6, 2021:

We're going to walk down to the Capitol and I'll be there with you. And we fight. We fight like hell and if you don't fight like hell, you're not going to have a country anymore.

This two sentence, twelve-second segment, represents the core of Trump's complaint. However, the issue with the statement is that Trump never said it. The above statement is actually two parts of a speech spliced together. Instead, the first remarks that Trump made were:

Now it is up to Congress to confront this egregious assault on our democracy. And after this, we're going to walk down and I'll be there with you. We're going to walk down, we're going to walk down. Anyone you want but I think right here, we're going to walk down to the Capitol and we're going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women, and we're probably not going to be cheering so much for some of them.

Nearly fifty-five minutes later, Trump continued:

[B]ut I said 'Something's wrong here, Something's really wrong, can't have happened.' And we fight, we fight like hell, and if you don't fight like hell, you're not going to have a country anymore.

Additionally, less than a minute later, Trump told his supporters to peacefully walk to the Capitol, stating:

I know that everyone here will soon be marching over to the Capitol building to peacefully and patriotically make your voices heard[.]

It is those two statements, edited and spliced together, that form the alleged defamatory twelve-second segment that aired in the Documentary. BBC admits Trump never made the statements as aired. The Chairman of BBC apologized to Trump, stating that the BBC "editing unintentionally created the impression of a single continuous section of your speech, rather than excerpts from different points in the speech." This, the BBC chairman stated, "gave the mistaken impression that you had made a direct call for violent action. That was an editorial error and it should not have happened." …

The court concluded that President Trump had adequately alleged actual damages and "actual malice" (i.e., knowing and reckless falsehood) on BBC's part, though of course the court noted that both would still have to be proved eventually as a factual matter. An excerpt:

For purposes of the defamation test, ill-will is different from actual malice. An intention to portray a public figure in a negative light, even when motivated by ill-will or evil intent, is not sufficient to show actual malice unless the publisher intended to inflict harm through knowing or reckless falsehood. However, ill-will or motive, when combined with other evidence, may be taken into account for actual malice….

Here, Trump alleges that BBC has a history of unfair or improper coverage toward him. In addition to the Documentary itself, Trump highlights the Prescott Memorandum, a 2022 BBC Newsnight episode, and the "2024 BBC News Shooting Hoax." As an important reminder, the state of mind required for actual malice must be "brought home" to the person in the BBC's organization responsible for the publication of the Documentary. This principle is relevant as it relates to the 2022 Newsnight episode and the 2024 "Shooting Hoax." Again, Trump has not alleged that either of these incidents involved the creator(s) of the Documentary. That said, these incidents are not merely portrayal in a negative light, but examples of BBC playing fast and loose with the factual accuracy of their media content. With respect to the Newsnight episode, the BBC seemingly did not care about the falsity of the portrayal until the later Documentary became an issue. Such examples can be said to be probative of BBC's state of mind as it pertains to recklessness in light of BBC's non-action toward false statements about Trump.

Thus, Trump paints a picture that demonstrates the BBC has a record of allowing the publication of false statements in their portrayal of Trump. BBC asks the Court to put on blinders and treat the Panorama team as if they were blocked off from the rest of the organization, ignorant of everything else going on at BBC. At this procedural stage [i.e., a motion to dismiss, where plaintiff must merely plausibly allege facts that could lead to liability, rather than proving them -EV], the Court simply cannot ignore the circumstantial evidence presented. To do so would make it extremely difficult to ever prove a defendant's subjective state of mind in any defamation case….

Trump alleged that BBC's editing of the speech was an "intentional and malicious effort to falsely and deceptively portray President Trump as having called for violence." In support, Trump alleges that it "would have been impossible for BBC's journalists and producers to splice together two distinct parts of the [s]peech from nearly fifty-five minutes apart unless they were acting intentionally." On its face, the editing may independently establish the plausibility of actual malice. BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a seventy-minute-long speech into twelve seconds. But the Court is not persuaded.

Editing is often required. However, given the time disparity between the two statements, the distance itself tends toward a plausible inference that BBC knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement. This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech. BBC also had the entire speech available to them for nearly three years by the time of the Documentary.

In addition to the editing itself, BBC's Chairman issued an apology:

The way the speech was edited in the documentary gave a misleading impression of what you said. The editing unintentionally created the impression of a single continuous section of your speech, rather than excerpts from different points in the speech. This gave the mistaken impression that you had made a direct call for violent action. That was an editorial error and it should not have happened.

However, the BBC now appears to disagree with the apology issued by the Chairman. BBC's Chairman admitted that the documentary gave a misleading and mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action. Strangely enough, BBC strays from that position in the Motion to Dismiss, referring to statements made by January 6 defendants as evidence that the speech may be interpreted as a call to violent action. But BBC's own Chairman acknowledged the editing was misleading in his letter to Trump….

As a final matter on the issue of actual malice, Trump alleges that BBC strayed from accepted standards of journalistic integrity. Such a claim on its own would not amount to actual malice, since actual malice requires "more than a departure from reasonable journalistic standards." A failure to investigate, standing on its own, does not indicate the presence of actual malice. To show actual malice, there must be some showing that the BBC purposefully avoided further investigation with the intent to avoid the truth.

BBC first argues that allegations BBC failed to contact Trump for comment before publishing are insufficient to establish actual malice. On this point, the Court agrees.

BBC then argues that allegations that BBC omitted portions of Trump's speech are also insufficient to establish actual malice. Alterations of quotes that "materially alter" the meaning of Trump's statements could support a finding of actual malice…. BBC did not just alter the quote but created a new quote by splicing two statements together and passing them off as a single continuous sentence. To the extent that there was no material alteration to the meaning of Trump's speech, that simply cannot be the case. The Chairman's letter makes it very clear that BBC acknowledges there was a material change of meaning when they edited the speech to create a single continuous segment that did not exist.

BBC then argues that the apology "militates against a finding of actual malice." … Today, retractions can be issued near instantaneously for online publications thanks to the internet. The Court acknowledges that media entities, like The Washington Post, or BBC, are not perfect, and make mistakes. However, it cannot be said that a retraction the next day is in the same ballpark as a retraction over a year later, and only after being threatened with legal action. The temporal distance here makes the retraction a weak indicator as to BBC's state of mind at the time of publication.

Further weakening BBC's argument, BBC was aware that such editing created a false impression as early as 2022. Former Acting White House Chief of Staff Mick Mulvaney, in relation to the 2022 Newsnight episode, stated on-air: "Your video actually spliced together the presentation.… [Y]our video makes it look like those two things came together." As BBC's own Clive Coleman stated "[t]he first lesson … you're taught as a broadcast journalist is that you do not joint two bits of footage together from different times in a way that will make the audience think that it is one piece of footage." Considering these facts, BBC's ultimate retraction in 2025 reads less like a readiness to retract, and more like a reluctance to retract.

The Court acknowledges that events from 2022 do not directly bear on the state of mind at the time of publication. But neither does a retraction over a year after publication. Hence why courts are often reliant on circumstantial evidence when making state of mind determinations. Still, Trump's allegations regarding BBC's departure from journalistic standards are more than enough to plausibly alleged more than mere negligence….

Of course, all of this does not prove BBC acted with actual malice. But it does make it plausible. And Trump need only allege facts sufficient to give rise to a reasonable inference that the BBC edited and published the Documentary "with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not." Trump has done so here….

And the court held the BBC's statement could be viewed as a false factual allegation, rather than merely "convey[ing] an opinion of what the audience understood Trump to say":

 As Trump correctly points out, a spliced segment that creates a sentence that Trump never spoke represents the exact kind of false statement of fact that courts hold as the sine qua non for recovery in defamation. Whether the audience "reasonably interpreted" the segment to convey that Trump called for violence is irrelevant….

The court also held that Florida courts (including the federal courts) had jurisdiction over the BBC. But the court rejected Trump's Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act claim:

… FDUTPA is limited to acts "in the conduct of any trade or commerce." The statute defines this as "the advertising, soliciting, providing, offering, or distributing" of goods, services, property, "or any other article, commodity, or thing of value." … "[M]agazines and newspapers often have commercial purposes, but those purposes do not convert the individual articles within these editorial sources into commercial speech." Both advertising and subscriptions are typical features of newspapers, whether online or in-print. Even if BBC has commercial purposes, that does not convert the Documentary into commercial speech….

Alejandro Brito, Ian Michael Corp, Jalaine Garcia, and Michael O. Mena (Brito, PLLC), Daniel Epstein (Epstein & Co.), Edward Andrew Paltzik (Tylor Dykema) represent Trump.

title: The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process
author: Stephen Wermiel
content:
One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.

This process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known. As we shall see, some of these questions have answers; others do not.

First, a review of the basics. The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60. By a 100-year-old tradition, review is granted when four of the nine justices want to hear a case. When this occurs, the parties file briefs and the justices hear oral argument before issuing their decision.

This process is a blend of transparent argument and secretive deliberation. The transparent portion is that the losing party in a lower court, the petitioner, files a public petition for certiorari, making the best case for why the court should resolve the legal issue in the case. The winner in the lower court, the respondent, also spells out why the court does not need to review the ruling of the lower court. After that, however, the case disappears into the halls and procedures of the high court.

Question one: how does the court handle and process the petitions?

As noted, by 100-year-old custom, it takes four votes for the court to agree to review a case (the “rule of four”). But the vote to grant or deny cert. is not public. We do not know if a petition met with overwhelming consensus that review was necessary or not, or whether it scraped by or just missed out on being granted.

Nor do we know why the court declines to review a case. When the court agrees to decide a case, the final opinion is likely to make clear why the justices were interested. Denials of cert. petitions, however, are not accompanied by any explanation, except in the few instances when an individual justice writes a dissent from the denial of a petition. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for example, sometimes points out in a dissent or concurrence what she deems to be an important issue of individual rights in criminal cases. But such dissents are relatively infrequent.

This can be frustrating to counsel: Just how much interest an unsuccessful petition attracted would be useful to lawyers trying to decide whether to petition the court in the future on an issue that has been turned down one or more times.

Question two: what roles do the law clerks and justices play?

The answer is known to some extent but secret in other respects. For seven of the nine justices – all but Justices Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch – the initial review is by a single law clerk who writes a memo to be shared with the seven justices who participate in a “pool” for reviewing the petitions. Clerks to Alito and Gorsuch handle the petitions on their own.

But much about this aspect of the process remains hidden from public view. Little is known outside the court’s inner circle about how the clerks prepare their memos and what factors influence their recommendation to grant or deny review. The court’s own internal Rule 10 says the court is looking for cert. petitions that either present a conflict in which two or more lower courts have reached differing interpretations of an important issue of federal law, or which, even in the absence of a conflict, present an important question that the court should decide. But those factors alone do not guarantee cert. will be granted.

Just how influential the memo writer’s recommendation is on the judgment of the justices is also unknown. Nor is there any public knowledge of how often justices think the pool memo reached the wrong recommendation.

The cert. pool has been in use by the court for more than 50 years. The justices are certainly able to make adjustments if they find flaws in how it works, and the separate handling of petitions by Alito and Gorsuch provides some check on the process. But since this is largely an internal procedure of the court’s own making, it is not subject to any public accountability.

And the justices rarely discuss it. In his new book, for example, Alito makes no mention of the cert. process or the pool. Ultimately, little is known outside the court about how individual justices handle the pool memos.

Question three: what influences the grant or denial or cert.?

Many factors besides Rule 10 might contribute to whether a petition is granted. Law clerks may be influenced by whether any of the most respected, regular Supreme Court practitioners are involved in the case. Clients certainly think this matters, since they may spend thousands of dollars to hire firms with top Supreme Court practices, those that boast having former solicitors general and former law clerks to the justices as members of the firm.

The clerks may also be swayed by what judges decided the case below, since some of them are especially respected in conservative or liberal circles. In certain instances, a federal appeals court may provide additional fodder to grant review. A party might have asked for rehearing by the full federal appeals court after losing in a three-judge panel. Such an “en banc” ruling, as it is called, can be especially influential, just as a set of opinions dissenting from denial of en banc review also tees up signals about the importance of a case.

Caution also plays a role here. No clerk wants to recommend that cert. be granted only to find that there are procedural flaws in a case (leading to it being “dismissed as improvidently granted”) or that the justices are not inclined to take up an especially ideologically divisive question.

Question four: why are there so few cert. grants?

The number of granted cases in recent years has reached the lowest level in many decades. At the height of the tenure of Chief Justice Warren Burger (1969-1986) in the 1980’s, the justices were deciding around 150 cases each term. Now the number is closer to 60.

Oddly, no one seems to know why.

There are some possible explanations, to be sure. One obvious factor is the rise of the interim docket, sometimes called the emergency or shadow docket. This docket involves interim requests for relief, where a party to a case asks the Supreme Court to block a lower court order in the interim period while the case is being litigated in a lower court. The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has used this path often, asking the justices to order that a Trump policy be allowed to remain in effect or to take effect after it was blocked by a federal judge.

These interim orders, decided without full briefing and oral argument, are taking up an increasing amount of the court’s time, and some argue that this leaves less time for the justices to add more cert. petitions to be decided on their merits. While this is undoubtedly a factor, the number of cert. petitions being heard by the court each term has been shrinking for a long time, well before the significant uptick in interim docket matters.

Different theories have been proffered by court observers for this decline over time: that Congress is passing fewer new laws that lead to lawsuits and require judicial review; that there is less disagreement between conservative justices and conservative lower court judges, so less need for review; or even that the justices simply like having fewer cases to decide and therefore vote for cert. more sparingly.

It is difficult to prove any one of these theories, and the justices are not providing any answers. In one case last spring involving a state court’s jurisdiction over a products liability lawsuit involving a company based outside the state, counsel for both sides agreed that the court should hear and decide the issue (a rare occurrence, as the winner below typically argues against cert. being granted), but the justices still denied the petition. As is typically the case, there was no explanation.

Question five: when does the court grant cert. before it is requested?

The Supreme Court’s Rule 11 and federal law allow the justices to essentially reach out and grant review to a cert. petition before it has been decided by the appropriate appeals court; that is, before the appellate process has run its course. This once rarely used process has become a much more frequent tool for the justices. Whether they are following the guidance of the rule and focusing on “imperative public importance,” or whether they are impatient to tackle some major legal issues, or whether they simply think it will be more efficient to leapfrog over the court of appeals, the practice is clearly on the rise.

A recent example is Trump v. Slaughter, a fight over the independence of the heads of federal agencies from being fired by the president. The federal government came to the court for an interim stay of the ruling of a federal district court in the District of Columbia that blocked Trump from firing Rebecca Slaughter, a member of the Federal Trade Commission, because there was insufficient cause. The court granted the stay, allowing the firing to take effect, and then also granted cert. and ordered the case to be argued in December 2025.

***

The process of granting review will continue unabated throughout the current court term. And as it does, questions will continue to arise about how the process works – but one should not hold their breath waiting for all the answers.

Recommended Citation: Stephen Wermiel, The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 12, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-sometimes-straightforward-sometimes-befuddling-certiorari-process/

title: Border wall decision caps busy Monday at SCOTUS
author: Blake Fox
content:
It was a busy Monday at the Supreme Court: the justices heard two oral arguments, released an order list, and decided the border wall dispute on the interim docket. Keep reading to catch up on these and other developments.

At the Court

On Monday, the Supreme Court granted the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that she would deny the request. Learn more about the dispute in the On Site section below.

Earlier on Monday, the justices heard arguments in two cases: Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations; and Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires.

Also on Monday, the Supreme Court denied review in over 200 cases, including disputes involving the George Floyd protests in Minneapolis, actor Randy Quaid, and the sons of former baseball player Roberto Clemente. It also asked the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a case over whether U.S. terrorism victims may sue 21 pharmaceutical and medical-device companies under the Antiterrorism Act for allegedly aiding and abetting Iraqi terrorists. For more on Monday’s order list, see the On Site section.

Today, the justices will hear argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC, on whether the Constitution allows the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – to adjudicate an employer’s obligation to comply with employment agreements concerning temporary immigrant workers.

On Wednesday, the Supreme Court Building will be closed in recognition of Veterans Day.

Recommended Citation: Kelsey Dallas & Blake Fox, Border wall decision caps busy Monday at SCOTUS, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 10, 2026, 9:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/border-wall-decision-caps-busy-monday-at-scotus/

title: GTA 6  reportedly has 55 Achievements/Trophies, more than both GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 had at launch
author: Dom Peppiatt
content:
You are gold.

GTA 6 is due to release on the 19th November on PS5, and Xbox Series X/S, and ahead of the highly-anticipated launch of Rockstar's latest sandbox adventure, people just can't get enough information about the game. To that end, overnight, we saw our latest leak: the game will have 55 Trophies/Achievements.

In a now-deleted tweet from (in)famous Rockstar dataminer, TexFunz2 - re-posted by the Twitter account iGrandTheftAuto - it appears the game will have 55 individual rewards for completing certain tasks and missions. At the time of writing, we don't know specifically what these challenges are, but it seems none of them will be attached to the online version of the game; the base game launches without GTA Online, and so we can safely assume that all these rewards will be for the single-player only content. GTA Online will drop sometime in 2027, according to Twitch's CEO.

If you've been paying attention to previous Rockstar titles, you'll know that Grand Theft Auto 5 launched with 51 Achievements/Trophies - again, all single-player - and Red Dead Redemption 2 launched with 52. So the latest game has more than either game got at launch - and I can tell you from experience, getting Platinum in either title was a very time-consuming experience. Expect the same to be true here, too.

It's worth highlighting that GTA 5 did, eventually, get more Achievements and Trophies: the GTA Online content upped the complete total to 78, adding 27 new challenges to complete. I would expect GTA 6 to do the same… whenever the PC version of GTA comes out, or GTA Online lands in the new game (it's possible both could happen at the same time).

Recently, we heard why a former Rockstar Games tech director thinks GTA 6 could be coming to PC sooner than you'd expect (mostly thanks to AI clones), when we can expect the pre-load of the game (10th November), and how big the final game install is expected to be (210GB). The final game is expected to be so big and dense with detail that no single Rockstar employee has seen the entire game, meaning there are plenty of easter eggs and ridiculous things to discover.
